STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
The Fifth Ministerial Conference of WTO held at 
Cancun, Mexico 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam, I beg to make 
a statement before this hon. House regarding the 5th Ministerial Conference of the 
WTO held at Cancun, Mexico during 10—14 September, 2003. 
The Cancun Ministerial Conference was due to take stock of the 
progress in negotiations under the Work Programme launched by the Doha 
Declaration and to provide guidance to negotiators on key areas such as 
agriculture, tariff negotiations for non-agricultural products, special and 
differential treatment and implementation issues. The Conference also had 
to decide on whether or not to launch negotiations on Singapore issues 
based on modalities agred to by 'explicit consensus'. 
In preparation for the Conference, the Government held wide ranging 
consultations with all major stake holders and had accordingly formulated its 
negotiating strategy. This strategy was based on an appreciation of our trade 
interests, development concerns and gains to be made by improving the 
multilateral trading system. We went to Cancun in a positive frame of mind 
with a desire to engage proactively in the negotiations for a fruitful 
outcome. 
The Conference which concluded in Cancun on 14th September, 2003 
could not reach a decision covering all areas. An important reason for the 
lack of a decision at Cancun was the inability of the proposals on the table to 
forge a consensus by taking into account the concerns of all Members on 
many contentious issues. The Conference ended with a Ministerial Statement 
which recognized that more work needed to be done in key areas to enable 
WTO Member countries to proceed towards the conclusion of negotiations under 
the Doha mandate. 
The developments at Cancun have been a disappointment for us. We are 
interested in having a healthy, effective multilateral trading system which would 
provide the institutional backdrop for a process of economic development that 
would benefit all countries. The overriding priority and 
384 
 

 
[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
consideration for a developing country like India in any trading arrangement 
is the implication of such an arrangement for its economic development. 
This focus on development determines our position on any trade rules 
and proposals at the WTO. Our goal at Cancun on major issues was 
guided by national interest. 
In agriculture, our desire was to ensure that agriculture markets across 
the world are freed from the substantia l distortions that are caused by 
large scale subsidisation. These di stortions prevent agriculture from 
fulfilling its potential of being an engine of growth. Income inequalities 
caused so far by such distortions continue. It is essential in the interests 
of equity, justice and fair play that the distortions in agriculture are 
gradually eliminated. Therefore, agricultural market access in developing 
countries has to be sequenced appropriately with reductions in market 
distortions elsewhere. At the same time, we wish to protect the interest 
of the millions of subsistence level farmers who depend on agriculture as 
their sole means of sustenance. Therefore, there has to be a calibrated 
approach to market access vis-a-vis reduction in distortions in agriculture 
with a transition period in which affected farmers are shielded through 
the use of special safeguard mechanisms and protection for special 
products. In view of all this, expecting us to make onerous market access 
commitments inconsistent with the reality in agriculture was unreasonable. 
The draft modalities on agriculture proposed at Cancun, on the other 
hand, did not take into account these concerns fully and would in all 
probability, have perpetuated distortions. We had no choice but to oppose 
these modalities. 
On tariff negotiations in non-agricultural products, significant 
convergence in negotiating position s could be realized by taking on 
board the concerns of all Members. 
On Singapore Issues, one has to address the question of multilateral 
rule making taking primacy over economic development goals, particularly 
in areas where the interplay between these new issues and development 
is unknown. The Ministerial Conference had to take a decision on 
modalities for all the Singapore Issues. However, this was to be by explicit 
consensus. Discussions clearly revealed that not only was this consensus 
absent but that most developing countries felt that the clarification process 
on these issues had not run its full course. In the absence of clarity on 
many elements, a majority of the membership for the WTO had rejected 
385 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 20031 
launch of negotiations on these issues and sought a continuation of the 
clarification process. There were concerns that a framework on Investment would 
constrain the policy space for developing countries in utilizing FDI for their 
developmkent goals. There was no certainty that such a framework would 
lead to larger FDI flows nor was any need for a framework demonstrated. On 
Competition Policy, the issue of encroaching upon the freedom of competition 
authorities was disquieting. The benefits of a framework on Transparency in 
Government Procurement were also not clear. In spite of this, proposals tabled 
suggested launch of negotiations in some areas. In the absence of explicit 
consensus, launching negotiations was however, an impossibility. 
India was disappointed that no time frame was prescribed for resolving 
outstanding implementation issues. These issues highlight the imbalances arising 
out of the Uruguay round agreement and need to be addressed on a priority basis 
so that imbalances brought in by the Uruguay round are redressed. On Special 
and Differential Treatment Issues, India felt that adequate urgency was not 
being shown in addressing these issues. 
An important outcome from our viewpoint is the engagement of 
developing countries in the negotiating process. Unlike in the past, when they 
were blamed for non-participation, the degree of participation of the large group 
of developing countries is a welcome development. Not only having developing 
countries become participants in the process but have also shown adequate 
flexibility to reach out to other fellow countries to form alliances which have been 
formed during and after the conference. The G-20 on Agriculture and the G-16 
on Singapore Issues embody the desire of developing countries to generate 
common positions on issues. 
The Ministerial Conference concluded with a Ministerial Statement which 
recognised that more work needed to be done in some key areas to 
enable WTO Member countries to proceed towards the conclusion of 
negotiations under the Doha mandate. The Ministerial Statement has 
instructed officials to continue working on outstanding issues with a renewed 
sense of urgency and purpose and taking fully into account all the views 
expressed in the Ministerial Conference. The Chairman of the General 
Council of the WHO, working in close coordination with the Director General, 
has been asked to coordinate this work and to convene a meeting of the 
General Council at senior 
386 

[22 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
officials levels no later than 15th December, 2003 to enable successful 
and timely conclusion of the negotiations. 
As Hon. Members would appreciate, trade negotiations are a 
protracted process. We have been engaging constructively in the 
negotiations and are optimistic that despite the lack of progress at the 
Cancun Ministeral Conference, it w ould be possible to move forward 
in the weeks to come. Agriculture has been at the core of the 
negotiations. Our sensitivities on Singapore Issues also need to be 
understood. We also committed to ensuring the 'development' lies at 
the core of the Doha agenda, as mandated at the Doha Ministerial 
Conference of WTO. 
For India, the multilateral process is an extremely important one. 
We believe that a rule based trading system provides a fair, transparent, 
predictable, secure and durable enviropment for trade relations between 
nations. We have been demanding that the system be fair-fair to our 
development goals, to our economic needs, to our economic and social 
reality and to our aspirations. The multilateral system continues to 
enjoy our support and we are partici pating in the process of further 
negotiations in Geneva. We are willing to work together and engage in 
a process of give and take so that  mutually acceptable outcomes may 
be reached. Movement forward demands understanding and 
accommodation. Our only desire is that  the discussions be carried out 
in a more understanding and sensitive manner so that trade 
liberalisation does actually deliver the fruit of development.

*301.   SHRIRAJU PARMAR:†† 
SHRIR. K.ANAND: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to

*304. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER

(a) whether it is a fact that the storage capacity of major reservoirs of the 
country has come down drastrically due to excessive silting;

planning stage itself for accumulation of sediment in reservoirs. The sediment 
flows accumulate in the dead storage provided for the purpose and thus the 
sediment deposition, in general, do not affect the efficacy of the project during 
the planned life of the reservoir. The studies on Silting of Reservoirs in India have 
indicated that while in some cases the rates of actual sedimentation are slightly 
less than that assumed at the time of planning, in other cases it is on higher 
side.

Pradesh where "Capacity Survey" have been conducted are given in the 
statement-1 (See below)

*310.   PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:  
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has rejected 88 out of the 90 
proposals for new urban banks received in 2002-03; 
(b) if so, whether the cooperative banking sector has been under Reserve 
Bank of India scanner for over last two years; 
(c) whether in its report on trends and progress of banking in India in 2002-
03, the Reserve Bank of India has given details of a mechanism put in place to 
streamline the cooperative banking; and 
(d) if so, the other reasons for rejecting the 88 proposals? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRIJASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that out of 88 proposals for 
opening new Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) in the country, the Screening 
Committee constituted by RBI has recommended approval for only two 
proposals during 2002-03. 
(b) Urban co-operative banking sector in some areas was facing a certain 
level of criris on account of irregularities committed by a few UCBs which led to 
substantial losses. RBI was, therefore,  required to initiate specific regulatory 
and supervisory measures to address bank specific problems and to avoid the 
recurrence of irregularities. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India 
in 2002-03, details the measures and other regulatory initiatives taken by the 
RBI during the year. RBI has set up a Committee of experts to screen proposals 
for new UCBs. The Committee takes into account the policy environment of the 
concerned State, track record and integrity of the promoters, requirements under 
prudential norms and the state of urban banking in the concerned State. The 
Committee has not recommended approval for the remaining proposals for 
various reasons like lack of

Transfer of Red Fort to ASI 
*306. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of TOURISM AND 
CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Army has already transferred portions of the 
Red Fort to the Archaeological Survey of India; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the complete charge would be handed over to 
the Archaeological Survey of India very soon; and 
(c) if so, what steps have been taken by Government to conserve and 
restore the past glory oTthe Red Fort? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): 
(a) to (c) On December 22,2003 the Ministry of Defence/Army Headquarters have 
transferred the entire Red Fort monument to the Ministry of Tourism and 
Culture/Archaeological Survey of India. Previously, only about 30 percent of the Red 
Fort area was with the Archaeological Survey of India/Ministry of Tourism and 
Culture. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
A number of steps for conservation and restoration of the Red Fort have already 
been taken in the area which was previously in the possession of the Archaeological 
Survey of India and the remaining measures are in hand. 
The steps already taken include: 
1. A nauseating slum, known as 'Chor Bazaar', and an area with open 
urinals and closed drains, has been replaced by an enchanting park 
which stretches from the northen extremity of the Fort to the area 
fronting Raj Ghat. 
2. Similar treatment has been accorded to the vast uneven and uncared 
For area on Chandni Chowk side which has been converted into a 
beautiful national park—August 15 Park. 
3. The entire surface of the Fort walls—21,219 square metres—has been 
throughly washed and chemically cleaned. 
4. The 1.7 kilometre long moat w ith massive slush accumulated over 
the years has been cleared. About 23,000 cubic metres of debris, with 
a load of 3,500 trucks, has been lifted from it. 
5. About 2,200 square metres of pathways which were of flag stones and 
were subsequently damaged and replaced by 'morram', have been relaid in 
accordance with the original design. The shell plaster on the walls of 
Mumtaz Mahal, Rang Mahal, Hamma, which had peeled off, has been 
refixed. 
6. All the 23 red sandstone Ja//-windows, which had broken, have been 
remade and refixed. 
7. Diwan-I-Khas, Khas Mahal, Naubat-Khana, Tehkhana, too, have been 
restored to their old glory. 
8. The old underground passage to the Yamuna River Front, under the 
Musammam Burj, has been cleared and opened on the King Road side. 
9. A special treatment has been accorded to a virtually unknown baoli— 
step-well—which hides a small but an inspiring part of history of our 
freedom struggle. 
40 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
10. A new underground Ticket House' has also been constructed and 'Light 
and Sound Show' upgraded. 
The area (70 per cent) which was transferred yesterday by the Ministry of 
Defence/Army Headquarters to the Ministry of Tourism and Culture/ 
Archaeological Survey of India, would be planned for taking proper 
conservation and restoration measures. For undertaking necessary work in this 
regard, a high-level Advisory Committee has.been constituted and further action 
in the matter is in hand.

†*314. SHRI MOTILA L VORA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be  
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that ex-Govern or of Reserve Bank of India has 
expressed concern over the increasing fiscal deficit of the Centre and States;

productive expenditure in order to decrease fiscal deficit;

affected due to increasing fiscal deficit?

revenue deficit and reduction in fiscal deficit to 2 percent by March 2008.

increased significantly in the Central Government Budget for 2003-04.

2230. SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBAADSUL): (a) to (c) ECB guidelines and 
procedures are periodically reviewed by the Government in the light of 
prudent management of external debt, changing market conditions, sectoral 
requirements etc. In the background of developments in recent months, 
Government in November, 2003 carried out revisions in the existing ECB 
policy for a temporary period until further review and relevant press release 
was issued on 12th November, 2003. The following changes were made: 
(i) All ECBs shall be subject to the following revised maximum spreads 
over six months LIBOR, for the respective currency in which the loan 
is being raised or the applicable benchmark(s), as the case may be: 
Type of Projects Existing New

(ii) ECBs for meeting rupee expenditure under automatic route to be 
heclged unless there is a natural hedge in the form of uncovered 
foreign exchange receivables, which will be ensured by Authorised 
Dealers (ADs). Under the old ECB guidelines, there was no 
stipulation of compulsory hedging.

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) ECBs exceeding USD 50 million wo uld be permitted for the 
following end uses only (a) Financing import of equipment and (b) 
Foreign exchange needs of infrastructure projects. Under the old 
ECB guidelines there was no end use restruction for ECBs except 
investment in capital market.

allowed acess to ECBs or to provide  guarantees. However, this will 
not apply to Textile and Steel restructuring packages which have

2240. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps Government have initiated to curb insider-trading in 
Stock Exchanges; and 
(b) whether Government propose to give more teenth/powers to market 
regulator, SEBI in tune with the expanded mandate of the regular for 
safeguarding genuine investors' interests particularly small investors? 
"THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The Securities And Exchange 
Board of India (SEBI) regulates insider trading through SEBI (Prohibition Of 
Insider Trading) Regulations, 1992. R ecent measures taken to curb insider 
trading practices are: 
1. The SEBI Amendment Act, 2002 included specific provision 
prohibiting insider trading and substantially increasing the penalty which can be 
imposed for insider traditing to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of 
profits made, whichever is higher. 
2. In order to create preventive mech anism for prevention of insider 
trading, the SEBI (Insider Trading) Amendment Regulations, 2002 provided 
for a model code of conduct to be followed by companies and SEBI registered 
intermediaries, and a code of corporate disclosure practices to be followed by 
listed companies. 
3. For detection of insider trading, surveillance mechanisms have been 
put in place by SEBI and stock exchanges. SEBI has further enhanced its 
surveillance through a regular system of weekly surveillance meetings with 
major stock exchanges and depositories to provide a platform for exchange of 
views on areas of emerging concerns and to consider pre-emptive actions and 
discuss general surveillance issues. 
(b) The SEBI Act, 1992 has been amended in December 2002 
including, inter-alia, many provisions seeking to further empower the 
regulator to protect the interests of investors.

Restoration of original structures in Delhi 
2289. SHRI RAJ KUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of TOURISM 
AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there are allegations against ASI for 
destroying the original structure in the garb of renovation of old historical 
monuments in Delhi; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to restore original shape of old monuments? 
166 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI 
JAGMOHAN): (a) to (c) In a public Interest Litigation filed in the Supreme Court, a 
few faults have been alleged about the nature of conservation and restoration work 
undertaken by the Archaeological Survey of India in the Red Fort, the Archaeological Survey 
of India/Government of India have refuted the alleged faults in a sworn affidavit and 
submitted that the entire restoration/conservation work has been carried out by the 
Archaeological Survey of India in accordance with the provisions of the Conservation 
Manual and well established norms as well as valid documents and old records which 
are in the archives of the Archaeological Survey in India. 
On December 22,2003, the Ministry of Defence/Army Headquarters have transferred 
the entire Red Fort monument to the Ministry of Tourism and Culture/Archaeological 
Survey of India. Previously, only about 30 per cent of the Red Fort area was with the 
Archaeological Survey of India/ Ministry of Tourism and Culture. 
A number of steps for conservation and restoration of the Red Fort have already 
been taken in the area which was previously in the possession of the Archaeological 
Survey of India and the remaining measures are in hand. 
The steps already taken include: 
1. A nauseating slum, known as "Chor Bazaar" and an area with open 
urinals and clogged drains, has been replaced by an enchanting park 
which stretches from the northern extremity of the Fort to the area 
fronting Raj Ghat. 
2. Similar treatment has been accordeed to the vast uneven and uncared for 
area on Chandni Chowk side which has been converted into a beautiful 
national park-August 15 Park. 
3. The entire surface of the Fort walls-21,219 square metres-has been 
thoroughly washed and chemically cleaned. 
4. The 1.7 kilometre long moat with massive slush accumulated over 
the years has been cleared. About 23,000 cubic metres of debris, with a 
load of 3,500 trucks, has been lifted from it. 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
5. About 2,200 square metres of pathways which were of flag stones 
and were subsequent ly damaged and replaced by 'morram', 
have,been relaid in accordance with the original design. The 
shell plaster on the walls of Mumtaz Mahal, Rang Mahal, 
Hamma, which had peeled off, has been refixed. 
6. All the 23 red sandstone Jali-windows, which had broken, have 
been remade and refixed. 
7. Diwan-I-Khas Mahal, Naubat-Khana, Tehkhana, too, have been 
restored to their old glory. 
8. The old underground passage to the Yamuna River Front, under 
the Musamman Burj, has been cleared and opened on the Ring 
Road side. 
9. A special treatment has been acco rded to a virtually unknown 
baoli-step-well-which hides a small but an inspiring part of history 
of our freedom struggle. 
10.    A new underground Ticket House' has also been constructed and 
'Light and Sound Show' upgraded. 
The area (70 per cent) which was tran sferred yesterday by the Ministry 
of Defence/Army Headquarters to the Ministry of Tourism and 
Culture/Archaeological Survey of India, would be planned for taking proper 
conservation and restoration measures. For undertaking necessary work in this 
regard, a high-level Advisory Committee has been constituted and further action 
in the matter is in hand.

country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATIBIJOYACHAKRAVARTY): (a) The per capita 
availability of water is not assessed State-wise. It is assessed river basin-wise. 
River basin-wise water availability and per capita availability of water is given at 
Annex. 
(b) As per international criterion, the annual per capita availability of water 
of less than 1000 cubic metre is considered as scarcity condition. 
(c) As per Narmada Water Disputes  Tribunal Award, the annual 
utilizable quantum of Narmada water (at 75% dependability), which will 
become available to Gujarat from the Sardar Sarovar Narmada Project, is 
11,101.32 million cubic metres (9.00 million acre feet (MAF). Thus the 
utilization of water will increase by about 11,101.32 cubic metre and by 
dividing the same with the total population of Gujarat, the per capita increase 
in utilization of water as a result of construction of Sardar Sarovar Narmada Dam 
works out to be of the order of 219.4 cubic metre. 
(d) To meet the projected water requirements, a live storage capacity of 177 
billion cubic metre (BCM) has already been created. An additional live storage 
capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the ongoing projects, 
Besides, proposals for additional projects are also under formulation consideration 
for creation of storage capacity of 132 BCM. To accelerate creation of irrigation 
potential by early completion of ongoing schemes, Government of India has 
launched Accelerated Irrigation Benefits

Development, for which technical and financial assistance is provided to the State

Water supply for agriculture 
2316. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 80 per cent of the total water supply in our 
country is used for agriculture against 70 per cent in the world; 
(b) whether considering the large amount of water used for irrigation as 
India's irrigated area is more than 20 per cent of the world area under irrigation, 
there is an urgent need for conservati on and efficient use of these resources; 
and 
(c) if so, what are Government's reaction thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) About 83% of 
utilizable water in the country is being used for irrigation at present against 69% in 
the world. 
(b) and (c) Yes, there is an urgent need for conservation and efficient use of 
water resources. The National Water Policy adopted by the Government of 
India in 2002 stipulates that "efficiency of utilisation in all the diverse uses of 
water should be optimized and an awareness of water as a scarce resource should 
be fostered. Conservation consciousness should be promoted through 
education, regulation, incentives and disincentives. The resources should be 
conserved and the availability augmented by maximizing retention, eliminating 
pollution and minimising 
192 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
losses. For this, measures like selective lining in the conveyance system, 
modernisation and rehabilitation of existing systems including tanks, 
recycling and re-use of treated effluents and adoption of traditional techniques 
like mulching or pitcher irrigation and new techniques like drip and sprinkler 
may be promoted, wherever feasible." The Prime Minister has also made an 
appeal to the Nation for making water conservation a National Mission. The 
Government encourages various measures for conservation and efficient use 
of water. 
Water consumption in Thermal Power Plants 
2317. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per a recenty study on water resources in our 
country, Thermal Power Plants consume 87.87 per cent of the water consumed by 
the industry; 
(b) whether it is fact that this water is consumed inefficiently and the 
consumption per power unit is 8 times that of international standards and costs a 
pittance; and 
(c) if so, what are Government's reaction thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) As per 
assessment made by the "National Commission for Integrated Water 
Resources Development Plan", the consumption of water by Power Plants is about 
30% of that by the industries. 
(b) Thermal Power Stations consume relatively higher amount of water 
for condensation of steam and for cooling of auxiliaries and ash disposal. 
Most of the old power stations have a once through cooling system where 
though large cooling water is drawn from the water body and most of it is 
discharged back to the water body after circulation through the cooling system. As 
such, a very small quantity of 2-3% of the total water drawn is actually 
consumed. Due to ambient conditions of higher temperature, heat rejection in 
stations in India is higher which increases the cooling water requirement. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
(c) Following steps are taken to conserve water used in power 
stations:— 
(i) As per Ministry of Environment and Forests, it is necessasry for all 
new stations to provide closed cycle cooling water systems where 
only a very small quantity of cooling water (2-3%) of the once-
through system is drawn from the water body for make up 
purposes. Zero discharge concept is also being adopted wherever 
possible. 
(ii) To reduce consumption of water for ash disposal, ash water 
recycling system is being provided in all the power stations. 
Further the utilisation of ash has been made mandatory and the 
utilities have been directed by Ministry of Environment and 
Forests to achieve 100% ash utilisation within a stipulated period. 
This will reduce the consumption of water in thermal power 
stations for ash disposal. 
(iii) In case of coastal locations, seawater is used for condenser 
cooling. 
(iv) Further, new techonology means such as dry cooling of 
condensers etc. are being considered for optimizing cooling water 
requirements of Thermal Power Stations.

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Kamaraj. 
*SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Madam, Deputy Chairperson, on behalf 
of AIADMK, I wish to make a few points on the Indian Telegraph (Amendment) 
Bill, 2003. The purpose of this Amendment is to increase the tele density in the 
rural and remote areas of the country at an affordable price. But the am ending 
clause 2 sub-clause (1) states, 'Fund means the Universal Service Obligation 
Fund.' Since the very purpose of this Bill is to provide telephone connection to 2.9 
lakh villages in the country, naming the fund as Universal Service Obligation 
Fund is not proper. Universal would mean that this scheme is meant for one and 
all. Therefore, I request the Hon'ble Minister to reconsider and name it Rural 
Service Obligation Fund. 
Madam, it is not possible to implement this scheme by collecting 5% of 
the revenues earned by the operators under various licenses as recommended 
by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India. The increasing population will demand 
more connections in the years ahead. It is difficult to implement this without fixing 
a target year. I think it would be better if the Government provides the entire 
fund as grant so that the scheme is not delayed. I appeal to the Hon'ble Minister 
not to delay if any further. The very fact that the Government has proposed to 
collect 5% of the revenue earned by urban operators for this fund shows the 
indifference of the Centre towards this scheme. I am pained to say that though 
a policy decision was taken to implement this scheme, no action was taken during 
the period between 1999 to 2003. 
Madam, we have seen that the conditional Access System could not be 
successfully implemented because the states were not consulted. Any scheme 
that is meant to benefit the people  at large ought be implemented in 
cooperation with the State Governments. This scheme also needs such 
consultation with the states for a total implementation. The New Telecom Policy 
of 1999 stated that telephon e connectivity to the backward areas, internet 
connections to all the district headquarters and telephone on demand would be 
provided in both rural and urban areas by 2002. But this has not happened as 
expected. I appeal to the Hon'ble Minister to implement the declarations without 
delay.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION— 
THE FAKE STAMP PAPERS SCAM IN THE COUNTRY INVOLVING 
SEVERAL THOUSAND CRORES OF RUPEES 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): On the question 
of stamp papers discussion, I have to very briefly share with the hon. Members 
that so far as the Ministry of Finance is  concerned, we administer, the Ministry 
of Finance administer the Indian Security Press, Nashik and the Security 
Printing Press, Hyderabad These two are the units that supply judicial, non-
jodicial and other stamp papers to the States and the Union Territories. The 
administering is on the authority of an Act— The Indian Stamp Act, 1899. States 
can have their own Stamp Act and some States like Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Gujarat, etc., do have their own Stamp Acts. All revenues from stamp duties 
accrue to the State Governments who decide who is to be licensed as a stamp 
vendor, method of collection, record keeping, accounting and all other such such 
related aspects. Now, I wish to share with the hon. Members the chronology of 
events of the entire stamp paper matter. One is that on 5th of March, 1998, 
sale of a perforating machine to an enterprise called the Unique Enterprises, 
took place. This is a routine exercise which is undertaken when machines get 
old; they are replaced with new ones and the old machines are sold through 
an auction, but the requirement, the entire conditionalities of sale require that 
they be destroyed, the cipher be destroyed, the blocks be destroyed and thereafter, 
the machine be disposed of. So, as I said on 5th March, 1998, before the 
National Democratic 
371 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
Alliance Government was shown in office, one of the machines was sold. On 1st 
April, 1998, soon after the National Democratic Alliance was sworn in, two more 
perforating machines were sold to the Unique Enterprises. About a year-and-a-
half later, in November of 2000, first reports of forgery, because of the Co-
ordinating Committee meetings, appeared in stamp papers and there was, at 
that stage, in November, 2000, no indi cation of any organised racket or 
involvement of any of the Security Press officials. In July of 2002—it is correct and I 
said so in the other House also. An hon. Members has raised this query.—I was 
given the charge of the Ministry of Finance. And, I then received, within days of 
my getting the charge, a letter from Chief Minister of Karnataka who suggested 
in the letter that some foolproof measur es should be introduced in the Security 
Press, also suggesting that there existed or there could be alleging that there 
existed some liaison or nexus between the ISP personnel and this entire matter. 
However, in that letter, no ISP personnel had been named. Immediately 
thereafter, I, of course, had acknowledged the letter, but I was absolutely new to 
the Ministry and I hadn't any knowledge or any investigation hadn't taken place. 
So, what we did was that we made an im mediate reference of this issue to the 
Intelligence Bureau to maintain surveillance, additional surveillance, because the 
machinery that we had at our disposal in the Ministry of Finance was not adequate 
to do so. So, Intelligence Bureau was requested to maintain additional surveillance 
over the ISP and the CNP at Nashik. In August of 2002, the Ministry of Finance 
alerted all security agencies and the surveillance over the two Presses was 
further tightened. In October, 2002, the CISF, took some time because we made a 
request, the requisition to CISF. My in vestigations had es tablished that the 
security arrangements were not very satisfactory, even the para-military 
security. So, the CISF replaced in October, 2002, the Departmental security at 
Nashik. In the December of 2002, further streamlining of system was requested 
and in January, 2003,1 received letter again from the Chief Ministry of Karnataka, as 
also from Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh recommending certain additional 
features in the nonjudicial stamp papers. We then convened a meeting at Nashik 
with security agencies to review all the security arrangement all over again. In 
February of 2003, the Working Group recommendations on new features of the non-
judicial stamp papers were approved and one of the Security Press officials was 
suspended. In March, 2003,1 wrote, at length, to the Chief Ministers both of 
Karnataka and of Andhra Pradesh and again a further review of 
372 

[23 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the security arrangements. Likewise in  April, 2003, the General Manager of 
Nashik Press was transferred whereafter all Chief Secretaries were advised to 
report, to ensure vigilance regarding any false or fake stamp papers and to verify 
stock and vendors. In July, 2003, the Home Secretary— by then we had requested 
the Home Ministry also—held a meeting with the State Chief Secretaries and 
the Directors General of Police, and the General Manager of the Security Press 
was suspended alongwith two others, three Deputy General Managers were 
transferred away from Nashik. In August, I recommended the dismissal of the 
General Manager of ISP, and, this was sent to the Department of Personnel and 
Training. In October this year, the production with new features of the non-judicial 
stamp papers started, and, we began to supply this new feature stamp papers to 
Andhra, and, all States would hereafter be covered by July of next year. 
More officials have been suspended at Nashik. But as far as CBI is 
concerned, the CBI is at present investigating seven cases relating to the stamp 
paper matter pertaining to the States, namely, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Delhi 
and Andhra Pradesh. The CBI has been given the go-ahead by the Ministry of 
Finance to take suitable action against the Security Press officials, and, the 
Government of India is determined because it is a very important issue that all 
guilty are brought to book and punished without delay. The Government of India 
is also filing a representation so that all cases having inter-state ramifications 
about fake stamp papers are transferred to the CBI, and, requesting the State 
Police of Maharashtra and Karnataka to share all their documents and material 
collected during their investigations with the Central Bureau of Investigation so as to 
enable the CBI to investigate the full implications of this fraud all over the country. 
So, the way forward, Madam, is that we have to amend the Stamp Act, 
and, we have to introduce a modern technology for foolproof collection of important 
sources of revenue for the State Gove rnments and the Government is also 
considering how best to play a catalytic role in facilitating a system thereby 
dematerialisation of stamps with computer connectivity can be installed, and, if 
necessary, the Central Government would consider funds for the pilot phase to 
introduce a system which will encourage. 
We are clear, and, I wish to reiterate, though I said so on earlier 
occasions also, that citizens who executed documents on those papers 
373 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2003] 
will not be put to any inconvenience, or, harassment, and, if required, we will 
introduce necessary legislative changes in this regard. 
There is considerable speculation about the extent of fraud. I have said in 
the other House that the seizure of fake stamp papers is about Rs. 3,500 
crores. I wish to, in all honesty, share with the hon. Members that various figures 
are now cited. From Rs. 35,000 crores, Rs. 30,000 crores, Rs. 60,000 crores. 
Please reflect for a moment, that if Rs. 60,000 crores of fake stamp papers were 
in circulation, and, have been utilized, then it would mean that the magnitude of 
the transaction on those stamp papers is over Rs. six lakh crores. It is absolutely 
impossible. It is highly improbable and entirely speculative figure, which really 
results in great deal of needless anxiety being caused in the citizens. There is a 
wrong that has taken place. The wrong must be corrected. The guilty must be 
punished. But, it is necessary that, at l east, in Assemblies, like the Parliament, 
we should be very careful about the figures we cite in regard to this entire 
matter. 
[MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
The CBI and the Income Tax Authorities are already investigating the 
matter, and, I have said in the other H ouse, that the Inco me Tax Department 
has taken a number of measures, and, some 47 odd properties have been 
seized. The solution to all this to myself lie in handing over the entire matter to the 
Central Bureau of Investigation, and that the future lies in dematerialisation of 
stamp papers, modernisation, and this kind of system that we have in which 
everything has to be on a stamp paper, progressively we have to get away from 
it. But the States, which have individual Stamp Paper Act, have also to reflect on 
this. I do believe, Sir, that this addresses all the significant or major query that 
were raised by the hon. Members in this regard. Thank you.

MR. CHAIRMAN. Hon. Members, we come to the close of the Winter 
Session which had commenced on Tuesday, the 2nd December, 2003. Indeed, 
it was a landmark being the 200th Session of the House. With a

than 50 years, we rejoiced in solemn celebrations with a view to recommitting 
ourselves to further serve the cause of democracy and work together towards 
fulfilling the aspirations of the people as well as their welfare. As part of the 
celebrations, a commemorative postage stamp was released; web casting of 
the proceedings of Rajya Sabha was inaugurated and a CD of a video film on 
Rajys Sabha was released. We also honoured all those Members, past and 
present, including a sitting Member, Shri Pranab Mukherjee, who had 
participated in more than hundred Sessions of the Rajya Sabha. We also 
honoured our distinguished colleague, Shrimati Najma Heptulla, for being the

This Session was short; we had 16 sittings, spread over around 68 
hours. The winter has been mild. The atmosphere in the House has been 
warm and cozy. Yes, we had occasional moments of emotional outburst, but 
the elderly graces and soothing words from the leaders always helped in 
overcoming the cordiality barriers. We, therefore, succeeded in doing substantia' 
business during the Session. 
During the Session, 320 Starred Questions and 2317 Unstarred 
Questions were admitted and answered. Three references from the Chair were 
made regarding "Twin bomb blast in Mumbai on 25th August, 2003", "Kumbh mela 
stampede in Nashik", and "Second anniversary of terrorist attack on Parliament 
Building on 13th December, 2001". The House also unanimously adopted a 
Resolution moved by the Chair, condemning the recent incidents of violence in 
Bihar, Assam, Maharashtra and in some other parts of the country in the wake of 
Railway recruitment examination and resolving to protect the regional harmony, 
unity and integrity of the country. 
The hon. Members also very effectively used the mechanism of Special 
Mentions to raise urgent issues of public importance. During the Session, 104 
Special Mentions were made I am also happy that status of replies by the 
Ministries to Special Mentions made in earlier Sessions has substantially 
improved. I would like to compliment the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs for 
effective follow-up which has brought about this improvement. I would urge 
sustained follow-up on pending cases. 
In this Session, substantia! Legislative Business was conducted; in

OBSERVANCE OF SILENCE IN MEMORY OF THE FATHER 
OF THE NATION AND OTHERS WHO GAVE THEIR LIVES 
IN THE STRUGGLE FOR INDIA'S FREEDOM 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today is 30 th January, the 
Martyrdom Day of Mahatma Gandhi, the Father of the Nation. Before we 
take up today's agenda, I request Member s to rise in their places and observe 
silence for two minutes in his memory and all those who gave their lives in 
the struggle for India's freedom. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to 
the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh and Shri Ramakrishna Hegde, 
former Members of this House. 
Shrimati Pratibha Singh passed away on 8th January, 2004 at the age 
of 75 years. 
Born at Salemgarh, District Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, in July, 1929, 
Shrimati Singh had her education at Women's College, Patna. 
An active social and political wo rker, Shrimati Singh took keen 
interest in the uplift of Harijans and welfare of women and children. She was 
also associated with various social  and welfare organisations and was 
instrumental in the establishment of  "Saket Home for Handicapped" in 
Chandigarh. She started the scheme fo r Indian Holiday Home at Taradevi 
near Shimla.   She was President of the Child Welfare Council, Punjab and 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [30 January, 2004] 
Red Cross Society, Punjab, from 1953 to 1958. She attended the Inter-
Parliamentary Conference at Berlin in the year 1986  and was Member of the 
Indian delegation to the United Nations in 1982. 
Shrimati Pratibha Singh represented the State of Bihar in this House 
for four consecutive terms from Decembe r, 1970 to April, 1976; from April, 
1976 to April, 1982; from April, 1982 to April, 1988 and again from April, 
1988 to July, 1992. 
In the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh, the country has lost 
a distinguished social worker and a noted Parliamentarian. Shri Ramakrishna 
Hegde passed away on the 12th January, 2004 at the age of 78 years following 
brain haemorrhage. 
Born at Siddapur, District North Kanara, Karnataka in August, 1926, 
Shri Hegde had his education at SIRSI, Kashi Vidyapeeth, Banaras and the 
Lucknow University. 
A lawyer by profession,  Shri  Hedge plunged himself into the 
freedom struggle and was jailed during the 'Quit India Movement' in 1942. He  
took  keen  interest  in  the  fields  of photography,  acting  in  movies, 
literature, fine arts and music. 
Suave and soft-spoken, Shri Hegde had a long and distinguished 
political career. He started his political  career with the Membership of the 
Karnataka Legislative Asse mbly in the year 1957 and was again elected to 
that Assembly in the years 1962, 1967, 1983, 1985 and 1989. He was a 
Deputy Minister in the Government of  Karnataka in the year 1957 and was 
Cabinet Minister in the State Government between 1962 to 1971, holding 
portfolios of Youth, Welfare and Sports, Cooperation, Industries, Planning, 
Panchayati Raj, Development, Information and Publicity and Excise and 
Finance. He was a member of the Karnataka Legislative Council from 1972 to 
1978, and was the Leader of the Opposition during that period. Shri Hegde 
became the Chief Minister of Karnataka in the year 1983 and held the post till 
September, 1988. As Chief Minister, he introduced many welfare schemes for 
the benefit of the weaker sections of th e society, backward classes, Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes and minorities. Known for his 'value-based 
politics' he also established the institution of Lokayukta for the first time in 
India to enquire into charges of corruption against Ministers including the 
Chief Minister. 
Shri Hegde represented the State of Karnataka in this House for two 
terms from April, 1978 to May, 1983 and from April, 1996 to April, 2002. 
2 

[30 January, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
He also served as the Union Minister of Commerce from 1998 to 1999. She 
Hegde also had the distinction of serving as the Deputy Chairman of the 
Planning Commission of India from 1989 to 1990. 
Shri Hegde was General-Secretary of  the All India Janata Party for 
six years. He was also the Vice-Presid ent of the Janata Dal and the Founder 
President of the Lok Shakti Party. He had several publications on varied 
subjects to his credit. 
In the passing away of Shri Ramakrishna Hegde the country has lost 
a distinguished and dedicated political worker, an eminent Parliamentarian 
and an able administrator. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh and 
Shri Ramakrishna Hegde. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Secretary- General will convey to the 
members of the bereaved families our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

REFERENCE TO VICTIMS OF EARTHQUAKE AT BAM IN IRAN 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members; the House expresses its heartfelt 
sympathies and condolences to the frien dly people of Iran on the suffering 
caused by the devastating earthquake which hit Bam on the 26 th December, 
2003. More than 35,000 people are feared dead while thousands of people are 
injured. Immense damage was caused to properties. 
This House notes that the Government of India has committed 10 
million US dollars towards relief assistance to the victims of the earthquake. 
The Government of India was quick to send a team of doctors which set up a 
field hospital at Bam complete with medicines, equipments and surgical 
facilities. Other relief materials such as blankets and high protein biscuits 
were also sent for the disaster relief. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of those who lost their lives in this tragedy. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION 
Extension of the Winter Session of Parliament after its adjournment sine die 
on 23rd December, 2003 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, with 
your permission, I would like to draw the attention of the House and the 
Government to a matter which has been agitating our mind. 
Sir, the Winter Session of Parliament began on 2 nd December, after 
being summoned by the President of the Republic under article 85 clause (1). 
On 23rd December, the House was adjourned sine die by the hon. Chairman of 
the House. And we have been asked, un der your orders in Bulletin No. 4167, 
dated 21st January, to assemble on 30 th January. In between, we are hearing 
that the Lok Sabha is going to be di ssolved; Vote on Account is to be 
approved by the Lok Sabha; there will be  a premature termination of the Lok 
Sabha and the General Elections will take place.  I 
6 

[30 January, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
am unable to understand what prompted the Government to take this decision, 
keeping everybody in the dark. Gener al Election is not an unusual event. 
Premature termination of Lok Sabha is also not an unusual event. If I 
remember correctly, it happened in 1970;  it happened in 1977; it happened in 
1979. It has happened umpteen number of times; and, as per the 
parliamentary practice, it is the prerogat ive of the Prime Minister to decide it. 
He can recommend to the President the dissolution of the House and the 
President can dissolve the House, in ex ercise of the power conferred on him 
by the Constitution. But what is the rationale behind extending the Winter 
Session? Approval of the Vote on Accoun t because the full Budget cannot be 
placed before the House due to General El ection, is not an unusual thing. My 
colleague, Dr. Manmohan Singh, who is sitting on my right, had presented the 
Vote on Account in 1996. He did not present the full Budget. That was the 
election year. We have seen it on a numb er of occasions that the Vote on 
Account is approved by the Lok Sabh a normally in an election year, if the 
elections are held earlier. If I remember correctly, in 1971, the Vote on 
Account was approved by Lok Sabha on 27-28 th March. It had happened in 
1977. The new Government came into existence on 23 rd March and the Vote 
on Account was approved by the Lok Sabha. 
Now, the problem is that the Houses are adjourned sine die by the 
respective Presiding Officers. In regar d to the prorogation, which is a 
constitutional requirement, the Presidi ng Officers of both t he Houses have a 
role to play. My point is that the Government of the day, to fulfil its own political 
agenda, to serve its own political agenda, has used the offices of the Presiding 
Officers. What happens normally in the case of prorogation is that after the 
House is adjourned sine die - after a couple of days - the Secretaries-General 
of the respective Houses enquire from the Government, from the Minister of 
Parliamentary Affairs, as to when the Government is going to prorogue the 
House. The President cannot prorogue th e House on his own. He requires an 
advice from the Council of Ministers, fr om the Prime Minister, as far as the 
summoning, the prorogation or the dissol ution of the House is concerned. If 
the Government had decided to hold elections, to terminate Lok Sabha 
prematurely, even then the Houses could have been called after the 
prorogation in the month of  January, or in the month of February, and after 
taking the Vote on Account, the House could have been dissolved. Heavens 
would not have fallen. In this case, we are doing away with another 
constitutional requirement which is under  article 87, clause 1. As per that, the 
President is to address the Joint Session of both 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [30 January, 2004] 
the Houses at the beginnin g of each year. Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is a little 
history behind it. Even the very first amendment of the Constitution in 1951 
took place on this issue. The original article 87 stipulated that each session of 
the Parliament was to be addressed by  the President. Therefore, after the 
adoption of the Constitution on 26 th January, 1950, when three sessions of the 
provisional Parliament took place,  every session was addressed by the 
President, and it was pointed out that it is inconvenient. So, the first 
amendment to the Constitution took pl ace in 1951 for amending article 87 and 
making a provision that the President will address only the first session of the 
year, and in an election year, as article 87 requires, the President is to address 
both the Houses after the new Lok Sabha is constituted. Therefore, the normal 
practice all these years is that in an election year, the President addresses 
both the Houses twice, once at the beginning of the year, when the first 
session takes place, and again when the new Lok Sabha is constituted. We 
understand that the Government wanted to hold the elections early and for that 
obvious reason it is the Executive's pr erogative, it is the Prime Minister's 
prerogative to do it. Everybody understands that. But, what is not 
understandable is, what would have happened if there was a normal session 
and if the President would have address ed it and if there was a debate on the 
Address of the President, which is the normal practice. Here the Members get 
the opportunity of reviewing the functi oning of the Government for the whole 
year which is contained in  the statement, in the Address of the Presidentl We 
are deprived of that opportunity. That st atement is not drafted by anybody else 
other than the Cabinet, and it speaks not hing else but the platitude of the 
Government. It may provide how India shines, how they feel good, and we 
have the opportunity to review the performance of the Government. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, especially in this year, it was required because the 
Winter Session was shortened. Since th is Government came to power, from 
1998 onwards, if you calculate the number of days of actual sittings, you will 
find that every time the days of Se ssions have been reduced. Those days are 
gone when Winter Sessions used to be for six weeks, Monsoon Sessions used 
to be for six weeks and Budget Sessions used to be for more than 12 weeks. 
This time also, we met in the Winter Session on 2 nd of December and we 
adjourned sine die on 23 rd December. We are deprived of having the 
opportunity of reviewing the performanc e of the Government which is being 
provided in the Address of the President, and the President is also deprived of 
addressing the two Houses of Parliament in the election 
8 

[30 January, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
year twice. He would not have given his own version; he would have given the 
version, as dictated by the Government. 
The third and the most important point  is - I charge the Government 
- that the institutions of Parliament have been mortgaged to the party's 
interests, to serve the party interests,  because the Government was not clear 
whether it would have early elections, whether it would dissolve Lok Sabha 
early. It was debated within the ruling party. They waited till 12 th and 13 th 
January when their national policy-making Body met. The Houses had been 
adjourned sine die on 23 rd December. They could have been adjourned on 
27th or 28th We were told and the whole country was told, *No, we are going to 
meet some times in mid-January, and you will have to wait to know whether 
we dissolve Lok Sabha, whether the Houses would be prorogued, or not. What 
is this? We are told not by the Government, not by the Ministry of 
Parliamentary Affairs, not by the Prime Minister as to when the Houses would 
be dissolved; but the party General Se cretary announced that on such and 
such date the Lok Sabha would be di ssolved; the party General Secretary 
assumes unto himself the responsibility of declaring what would be the time 
when elections would be held, to declare the election schedule, though the 
Lok Sabha has not yet dissolved and the Election Commission has not yet 
applied its mind. The ruling party's Genera l Secretary tells us that elections 
would take place on such and such date, the Lok Sabha would be dissolved 
on such and such date! The presiding officers have a minor role! 
As per the practice, as I mentioned,  it is the Secretaries-General of 
the Houses who would assertain from the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs or 
from the Leader of the House or from the Prime Minister as to when the 
Houses would be prorogued, and only after ascertaining this fact the 
Secretaries-General of the Houses - Secretary-General of Lok Sabha and 
Secretary-General of Rajya Sabha - send the communication to the Secretary 
to the President, and not the Cabinet Secret ary; not any other Secretary, as in 
this case. 
Therefore, that is  the practice which we have evolved. 
Unfortunately, there is no plausibl e explanation. I would expect the 
Government would explain what great difficulties they would have faced had 
they followed the normal practice? wh at great inconvenience the country 
would have faced? In between, we have seen - I am not going into the details 
because we will get an opportunity of di scussing those issues -technically, the 
House is in session but announcements are made giving 
9 

RAJYA SAiHA [30 January, 2004] 
concessions worth thousands of crores of rupees. They may feel happy; they 
may feel good; they may shine; but, there are certain Constitutional proprieties 
when the Houses are not prorogued, when a House is adjeurned sine die, 
when the Presiding Officers  can summon the Houses at any point of time, 
then, all these major announcements are not made. But, completely ignoring 
the fact that the House is in sessi on, major announcements have been made! 
Normally, the Ministers do not make any major announcements even on 
Saturday or Sunday. Mr. Chairman, Sir, you will recollect that even in a short 
recess period or weekend holidays - Saturday and Sunday or even if there be 
a holiday - no major announcement is made by any Government. 
You are claiming that since the Parliament is in session there is no 
need of issuing any summons, and that there is no need of application of 
article 87(1) because t he Presiding Officers are calling the Session. But 
announcements are made completely igno ring that fact Therefore, I demand 
from the Government an explanation on this issue. 
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need for Immediate Central Assistance to Tackle Unprecedented drought in 
Karnataka 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN (Karnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, Karnataka 
is facing unprecedented drought for the third consecutive year. During the entire 
period from January to December 2003, out of 176 Taluks, 161 Taluks in Karnataka 
have received less rains, causing deficiency of about 23 per cent rainfall in the 
State. In Septebmer and November 2003, the rainfall has been the lowest of the 
last 30 years. Due to dry spells, 42 pe r cent of the standing kharif crops and 
36.5 per cent of rabi crops have been affected. The total damage assessed for 
horticulture crop is Rs. 3974.39 crores. A delegation comprising members of 
the Cabinet Sub-Committee on Management of drought in Karnataka and 
Members of Parliament both from Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha met the hon. 
Prime Minister, the Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission and the Minister for 
Agriculture on 17th and 18th December, 2003 to personally apprise them about 
the seriousness of the prevailing situation of drought in Karnataka for the third 
successive year. Even after the strong plea made by the State Government, 
the Central Government has released only Rs. 115.86 crores as against the 
request of Rs. 1881.55 crores. On 29.12.2003, another 1.65 lakh metric tonnes of 
rice were released as against the request of 9.9 lakh metric tonnes. It is an injustice 
done to the poor farmers in the State of Karnataka. Therefore, I urge upon the 
Central Government to take immediate measures to provide requested financial 
assistance and release foodgrains immediately. I would request you to kindly 
see to it that the Government acts immediately.

Special Mention.

Mention pertains to the demand for freedom to earn livelihood by rickshaw and 
cart pullers, hawkers, vendors and petty mechanics and others in the country. 
At present, our country is passing through the worst phase of 
unemployment amongst the youth. Crores and crores of youngmen and young 
women are unemployed and are searching for jobs. The government jobs have 
become extinct. Even a decade ago I reme mber the youth used to be busy 
preparing for various competitive examinations of the SSC, UPSC, Banking 
Service Commision, State PSCs, etc., and they were getting jobs. But, now, 
competitive examinations are hardly held. On the contrary, the VRS has become 
the order of the day, and abolition of posts has become a routine in Government 
Departments and PSUs. Self-employment has become the slogan, but this is 
proving to be more difficult than getting a job. If a youth wants to earn his livelihood 
by pulling a cycle rickshaw, hand cart or he wants to sell vegetables, fruits and 
other articles as a hawker or a vendor or he sits by the roadside to repair cycles, 
scooters and other vehicles as a mechanic, it is just not possible for him to do so.

Threat posed due to import of toxic Industrial waste 
SHRI B. J. PANDA (Orissa): Sir, India is increasinglybecoming a preferred 
dumping ground for toxic industrial waste from developed countries, which poses a 
serious threat to our public health and environment. While developed countries 
have banned its use because of its devastating impact on their public health, we seem 
to think that we need every dollar and every job that is created out of it. The brain-
damaging mercury, toxic electronics, plastic wastes, cancer-causing asbestos, 
defective steel and tin plates, toxic waste oil, used batteries and scrap of metals 
from developed countries dumped on us have increased manifold. According to 
studies, every year, 1,00,000 tonnes of hazardous wastes enter India in gross 
violation of the 1997 Supreme Court order banning such import. Mercury causes 
severe and permanent damage to the central nervous system, lungs and kidneys, 
triggers depression and suicidal tendencies and causes paralysis. It has severely 
contaminated land, water, air and t he food chain throughout the country. Raw 
asbestos, banned in all developed countries, is imported to the extent of around 
one lakh tonnes per annum. It causes fatal diseases including lung cancer and 
many other ailments. Even in our Factories Act, 1948, asbestos has been listed 
as a disease-causing substance. More appalling is that while our country is now the 
major dumping ground of these hazardous wastes, Government has not thought it 
fit to regulate its trade and use. It is high time that India took a serious look into 
this problem to address this issue in our overall national interest.

November, 1967, the Government of We st Bengal was dismissed by the then

House or not. Ultimately, after a good deal of discussion, the House arrived at a 
decision, through the ruling of the presiding officer that 'the conduct of a 
Governor, in discharging his constitutional responsibility, could be discussed on 
the floor of the House1. Thereafter, in 1968,1969 and till very recently, on several

exercise of their constitutional responsibilities, those issues were debated and the 
Government had always taken the position that the Governors had acted in 
regard to the prorogation of the legislat ures on the advice of the Council of 
Ministers and that, therefore, the Governors were within their constitutional right.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Unemployment problem in the country 
SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal): Thank You, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for 
giving me an opportunity to participate in the short duration discussion on the 
unemployment problem in the country. 
May be, this is going to be my last speech to the Members of the 
Treasury Benches who are sitting on my left in their capacity. After some time, 
they may be sitting on my right. Therefore, I seek some compassion from you 
while speaking. The second thing,, Sir, is that I do  not know as to why the 
Labour Minister has come to hear and reply to such a critical issue which has 
become the most menacing issue to this nation, to this country. Now, job riots are 
taking place, and it is taking the form of linguistic riots in some of the places. And, 
policy questions are involved in it. What will be the direction of the ec onomy, 
whether the Government will make public investment or not, what will be its 
technology policy, etc.? I do not think the Labour Minister is in a position to reply 
to all those questions, and, hence, I would request that either the Prime Minister 
or the Finance Minister should reply to this debate because, this debate does not 
pertain to the Labour Ministry alone. I do not wish to make politics out of the 
unemployment problem that is prevailing in the country. But, Sir, the 
Government is playing with the poorest of the poor of this country by declaring 
everyday that every year they are giving employment to one crore people. That 
is simply rubbing salt to the injury of the poor and the unemployed youth. They 
should stop doing it. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK) in the 
Chair.] 
What is happening? My esteemed friends who are sitting on my right 
are hot the angels, but the fact is that  during the period between 1992-97, the 
number of registered unemployed people did not move for five years. It was 3.9 
crores in the year 1998, and around 2 lakh people 
31 

RAJYA SABHA            [3 February, 2004] 
were getting employment during that period. But, in 2000, the figure jumped up to 
4.16 crores and the rate of employment was only 99,000. Sic, the rate of growth 
of employment is declining, and the unemployment rate is increasing every year. 
Between 1983-94, the growth rate of unemployment was around 0.8 per cent; 
sometimes it was minus, it has gone down, that means, at least, a good number 
of people who were coming to the employment market were getting 
employment. But is it happening today? The growth rate has gone down from 2.7 
per cent of 1.07 per cent in 1998. And now, the Ahluwalia Committee have said 
that the growth rate is 'nil' so far as employment is concerned. Such a serious and 
dangerous situation had developed in the country and our Prime Minister is going 
on making statements everyday that one crore people are getting employment 
every year. Sir, I have seen many Prime Ministers. But I have not seen one who 
has acquired such a terrific virtue of lying to the people; I have not seen or heard 
any Prime Minister before that! The Planning Commission is saying one thing, the 
Finance Ministry Report is saying one thing, but he is un dauntingly going on 
saying 'one crore, one crore, one crore1 and thus, he is hurting the poor people 
and unemployed youth. 
Sir, Articles 41, 42 and 43 of our Constitution have said that the Directive 
Principles of State Policy will be to grant the right to work as a fundamental 
right. Though it was not given as a fundamental right, the Directive Principles of 
State Policy is to give right to work, right to education, as fundamental rights and to 
act towards that. That was the 'Directive Principles of State Policy' according to 
the Constitution. I wish to know from t he Government whether they still hold that 
opinion or they are going to change the Constitution itself. The thing is employment 
in the organized sector is going down at an average of one lakh every year. During 
the last four years, employment has gone down by four lakhs in the organized 
sector. Your report says so, and now, there is no increase or improvement in the 
employment situation. 
Then employment is going down at the Central Government, State 
Governments even the local self-Governments, and the public sector. But from 
where have those one crore people who got employment come? Are those people 
in the heavens or in the sky or on the ear th—Prime Minister should explain that 
position; your Government should explain that position.

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Madam, Mr. Singhal is 
right in saying that, perhaps, it has become a ritual to discuss about 
unemployment. It has become a ritual because, however seriously we may 
express our anxiety, whatever seriousness we may add to this problem, we 
cannot act, we cannot decide about the policies. It is the Government which 
has to take a lesson from this situation.  The Government has to resort to some 
policies so that a formidable solution could be arrived at in resolving this 
perennial problem of unemployment. 
(THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, DR. A.K. PATEL, in the Chair) 
Unfortunately, it has not happened. No proper action could be resorted to 
by this Government in the last four or five years. Even before the elections, the 
Government has pledged to the nation that it will generate at least one crore jobs 
every year. Now, we shall have to look at the balance-sheet. When the 
Government has decided to dissolve the Lok Sabha, when they are trying to 
absolve them from the responsibility of answering to the Parliament, we must 
look at the balance-sheet as to what exactly has happened. In fact, the situation, 
as on today, in so far as the unemployment problem is concerned, is deplorably 
poor. The hon. Labour Minister is sitting over here. He may, perhaps, agree with 
me that the unemployment situation or the employment situation is deplorably 
poor in the country of ours. It is very unfortunate that millions and millions of young 
men and women have been rendered unemployed or they are roaming around 
unemployed. There are no jobs at all. Even the Leader of the Opposition is saying 
that. Even the Planning Commission in its recent observation has stated that there 
are 21 crores of young men and women, in the country, between the age of 16 
years and 26 years, and during the intervening period of five or six years, hardly 
23.6 per cent of them could be employed, and that too, in the unorganised sector 
or in the informal sector. Only 9.6 per cent could be employed in the formal sector 
or in the organised sector where at least a minimum guarantee of jobs is there. 
Even then, the security of job is something which is completely missing during the 
regime of this NDA Government in the last three years. Sir, You will certainly 
appreciate that this unemployment problem is inextricably linked with the 
economic policy that this Government pursues. In fact, the Labour Minister has 
nothing to do with it. Here, in the morning, some of my revered colleagues raised 
this point that, in fact, the Labour Minister

RAJYA SABHA [3 February, 2004] 
was a poor man. He could not do anything because the Labour Minister was 
concerned with the problems of labour; he was concerned with the problems of 
workers. There also he has totally failed. Not only that he has failed but also the 
situation has become quite bad because, as of today, the increase in trade and 
investment has not translated into commensurate income increase, especially, for 
most workers, as per predictions. T he gains have been concentrated among 
the corporate houses and big companies. Their profits have increased as the 
purchasing power of the typical urban consumers have also increased. The poor

become poorer. The Government has also accepted that t he number of people 
living below the poverty line is not one or two lakhs. Their number is 34 crores. 
Out of a population of 107 crores, some 34 crores of people live below the poverty

about their livelihood? Nobody cares about them. This Government, at least, 
does not care at all. 
Sir, I must say that many committees have been formed. Of course, during 
the last 50—56 years, many committ ees have been formed. Many committees 
might have made some recommendations. Maybe, some of the 
recommendations were quite useful recommendations. But the Government, 
particularly, this NDA Government, has not at all considered those recommendations 
and acted in the right earnest to resolve the problem of unemployment. Moreover, 
during the last 4-5 years, the situation has become bad because the number of 
jobless is more than the number of jobs created. The job opportunities as such

been afraid of this situation. We have always said this. We have said this time 
and again. We tried to assert that this Economic Policy is going to lead us to a 
jobless and voiceless growth. Today, it has been vindicated. Our apprehension

am not talking only about the rural sector. It is also there in the urban sector. In the 
urban sector also unemployment has grown by leaps and bounds.
